new_statements.translation: Besides these, other conditions are also found in this district: 1. When (both syllables of) disyllabic words are long, the stress falls on the first: Panvari moṭho = stress on mo ... 2. When the first syllable is short and the following one long, the stress falls on the following syllable: Panvari muṅgī, uṛīd = stress on gī and ṛī ... 3. Stress falls on a geminated consonant: Panvari coṭṭin, ḍukkar = stress on ṭ and k ... 4. In a disyllabic word written with three letters, when the first letter (vowel) is short and the last long, the stress falls on the final syllable: Panvari jhunkī, haṭkā, muṅgsā = stress on kī, kā and sā.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is treated as weight-driven rather than positional: in disyllables with two long-vowel syllables the first is stressed; if the first syllable has a short vowel and the second a long vowel, the second is stressed; a syllable closed by a geminate attracts stress; in CVC.CVV-type words (short first vowel, long final vowel) the final syllable is stressed. Otherwise (p.108) stress is described as free and used mainly for emphasis/meaning contrast, with 'equal contrastive stress on all words' in a neutral sentence.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not discussed; p.108 only says that in polysyllabic words some syllable gets more and some less stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed as exceptions; the author frames stress as largely emphatic/sentence-level ('bhale hi vah kisi akshar par nishchit na hokar mukt ho' = though it is free, not fixed on any syllable, p.108) and gives the four weight conditions as additional word-level regularities with 1-3 examples each. Analysis follows the standard Hindi-dialectology (Mehrotra school) template; no instrumental support.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level rules illustrated on isolated disyllabic citation forms; the surrounding discussion (pp.107-109) is about syllable-, word- and sentence-stress used for emphasis and intonational meaning.
new_statements.identity_note: The source (Awasthi 1995) describes 'पंवारी (Panvari)' as spoken by the Powar/Panwar caste of Balaghat district, Madhya Pradesh, i.e. Wainganga-valley Powari = Grierson's 'Powari' of Balaghat/Bhandara = powa1246. It is NOT the 'Pawari/Bhoyari' of Betul-Chhindwara-Wardha (Bhoyar Pawars), which community writers and LSI IX-2 treat as a separate Malvi/Rajasthani-type variety (Ethnologue lumps it under pwr as 'Bhoyar Powari'). The thesis treats Panvari alongside two other Balaghat caste dialects (Lodhanti, Marari); only the Panvari examples are quoted here.

sources.locator: Ch. 2 ('Panvari, Lodhanti evam Marari boliyon ka vishisht adhyayan'), section 'balatmak svaraghat', thesis p. 110 (pdf p. 41 of 07_chapter); framing on pp. 107-108
sources.note: Ch. 2 'dhvani prakriya' has a suprasegmental section: musical accent/intonation (pp.105-107) and 'balatmak svaraghat' (stress) pp.107-110. Distinguishes sound-, syllable-, word- and sentence-stress; says stress is mostly used for emphasis/meaning change and is 'free, not fixed on any syllable' (p.108), then gives four word-level placement rules for Panvari (p.110): two long syllables -> first stressed; short+long -> second stressed; geminate consonant attracts stress; (C)VCV-CVV words with short first and long last -> final stressed.
